teaser: Twenty open AI governance controls under CC BY-SA, why the licence matters, and the same day's conversion into a graph, a database and a walk down to EU law.
core_idea: The AI Baseline Control Framework is a practical, deployer-focused set of twenty AI governance controls in five categories and three types, each with a why and a how and a mapping to the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act; its Access category covers what an AI system can reach, which the three it maps to do not; its CC BY-SA licence and CSV export let it be converted on the day into a semantic graph with an ontology, a taxonomy, linked data, documents and a browser database, joined by id to a graph of the AI Act, and walked as a fractal graph from the framework down to a paragraph of law, which surfaced findings the list does not state and kept every addition labelled apart from the source.

nodes.label: AI BCF: twenty controls for deployers
nodes.summary: Five categories, three types, a why and a how per control, mapped to NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the AI Act; v1.0, 2 October 2026.

nodes.label: Baseline, Tier II, Trigger
nodes.summary: Trigger controls apply only when a stated condition holds, which keeps the framework proportionate across organisation sizes.

nodes.label: The Access controls have no equivalent in the three
nodes.summary: AC.1 to AC.4: access reviews, named identities, accountable owners and the access model for AI systems themselves.

nodes.label: Grant, mandate and owner
nodes.summary: The Agent Behaviour Policy's words for what an agent can reach, what it may do, and who answers for it.

nodes.label: CC BY-SA 4.0 says yes in advance
nodes.summary: Share and adapt for any purpose with credit, changes indicated and the same licence on what is shared.

nodes.label: ShareAlike keeps the tools open
nodes.summary: A framework is worth the tools built on it; ShareAlike keeps shared tools as open as the framework.

nodes.label: A CSV export turned a reading into a dataset
nodes.summary: One row per control, sources in one column, a URL per control: the input for the whole conversion.

nodes.label: One CSV in, five shapes out
nodes.summary: A deterministic build writes a graph, an ontology, a SKOS taxonomy, JSON-LD and Turtle, eighty documents and a SQLite database.

nodes.label: Every edge says where it came from
nodes.summary: Source, structure, parser-derived, derived-join and overlay, shown in every view so additions are never mistaken for the framework.

nodes.label: Five altitudes, one grammar
nodes.summary: The graph view walks from the framework to a category, a control, a cited clause and the paragraph of the AI Act it resolves to.

nodes.label: Two vaults joined by matching ids
nodes.summary: AI Act citations resolve to the Regulation Graph's nodes because both graphs keep the same grammar.

nodes.label: The law links controls listed separately
nodes.summary: The AI Act's own cross-references connect four pairs of Comply controls by seven paths.

nodes.label: Four cited articles were amended in 2026
nodes.summary: Articles 4, 5, 27 and 50, amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; GV.3, CM.1, CM.2 and CM.4 are the controls to re-read first.

nodes.label: SQL and triples in the browser
nodes.summary: sql.js builds the tables in the page; a triple console asks the same graph from either end through declared inverses.

nodes.label: If the framework publishes its own graph
nodes.summary: It should be authoritative, and this vault should be superseded by it rather than merged into it.

quotes.why: The framework author's reply, and the input the whole conversion was built from.

quotes.text: A licence that permits adaptation in advance means each of those can be built, and shared, without asking.
quotes.why: Why an open licence matters more for a control framework than for most documents.
